# Quickstart

Get SEALS running, then make it your own. This picks up where
[Installation](installation.qmd) leaves off — it assumes you have an activated
environment with SEALS installed, either as the `sealsmodel` package from
conda-forge or as a developer's editable install from a clone. For what the
model actually does, see [Introduction](index.qmd).

## 1. Run it

Two run files ship with SEALS, in `seals/seals/`:

| file | what it runs |
|------|--------------|
| `run_seals.py` | the standard pipeline: three scenarios, 2030 and 2050 |
| `run_seals_test.py` | the same pipeline pared down — baseline plus one BAU, one year, Rwanda |

Start with the test. How you launch it depends on how you installed.

**Installed from conda-forge.** The run files live inside the installed package,
and a run file is not launched from there: it is launched from a project folder
of your own, which is also the folder your own work will grow in. Make one, with
an `input_template/` beside the run file:

``` bash
mkdir -p ~/Files/seals/seals_first_run/input_template
cd ~/Files/seals/seals_first_run
```

Download
[standard_scenarios_test.csv](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/jandrewjohnson/seals/main/seals/input_template/standard_scenarios_test.csv)
into `input_template/`, and save this beside it as `run_seals_test.py`:

``` python
import hazelbean as hb
from seals.run_seals import run_project

if __name__ == '__main__':
    p = hb.ProjectFlow(project_name='seals_test', run_mode='check',
                       extra_dirs=['Files', 'seals', 'projects'])
    p.scenario_definitions_filename = 'standard_scenarios_test.csv'

    run_project(p)
```

The pipeline itself is imported from the package; `extra_dirs` tells ProjectFlow
where to put the project directory, since there is no cloned repo for it to
infer that from. Then:

``` bash
conda activate <your_env>
python run_seals_test.py
```

**Developer install.** The clone already holds both files, so run the shipped
one in place:

``` bash
conda activate <your_env>
cd ~/Files/seals/seals/seals
python run_seals_test.py
```

Either way, required base data is downloaded at runtime from a public bucket;
no credentials are needed for the default configuration.

## 2. Where the output goes

Not beside the run file, and never into a repo. ProjectFlow places the project
directory under `~/Files/seals/projects/` — inferred from the clone's location
for the developer install, and named by `extra_dirs` for the conda-forge one:

```
~/Files/seals/projects/seals_test/
├── input/          your override copies only (the repo's input_template/ is read in place)
├── intermediate/   one folder per task
└── output/
```

Run the same command a second time and it finishes almost immediately — every
task is behind an existence check, so completed work is skipped. That is the main
thing ProjectFlow buys you: interrupt a long run, fix one input, re-run, and only
what is missing recomputes.

## 3. Make it your own

Copy the run file into your own project repo as `run_<project>.py` and change the
two lines in its `__main__` block — that is the whole of the configuration. (If
you installed from conda-forge, step 1 already put you in a project folder with
exactly this shape.)

``` python
if __name__ == '__main__':
    p = hb.ProjectFlow(project_name='my_project', run_mode='check')
    p.scenario_definitions_filename = 'my_project_scenarios.csv'

    run_project(p)
```

`run_mode` controls how much prior work is reused: `'check'` (the default)
resumes in a stable project dir; `'full'` timestamps a fresh one.

Put your scenarios CSV in an `input_template/` directory beside the run file. It
is tracked in git and ProjectFlow reads it there in place; a copy you place in the
project's untracked `input/` shadows it. Make the project folder a git repository
and ProjectFlow infers the project directory from it, so `extra_dirs` becomes
optional. The
columns are documented in
[Custom scenarios](custom_scenarios.qmd).

To run the same pipeline a second way — a smoke test, a different AOI — write a
*second run file* that imports the first rather than copying it.
`run_seals_test.py` is the worked example, and the pattern is explained
in [conventions](https://justinandrewjohnson.com/earth_economy_devstack/conventions.html).
